subject: City Budget
comment: Spencer Stevens Email Dear City Council, My name is Spencer Stevens, and I have been a resident of Salt Lake City for 2 years. I'm writing direct to the council, and I am grateful for all that is being done on behalf of community members like me. However, I write regarding the budget for 2022-23, and I wanted to make sure community members like me are heard. Housing: speaking to both the homeless and non-homeless citizens of Salt Lake City. Although there are complications in obtaining building materials for new housing, I believe we can work with what we have as well. For instance, I live by the Gateway area, and there are areas of available space that can be used for affordable housing opportunities that I believe the city can work with landlords and developers on. Additionally, working with not-for-profit partners can help with the ongoing economic and social vitality of our community. And yes, I would say this especially includes providing stable housing for the homeless. Though homelessness is a complex issue, there is quite a bit of data to demonstrate that stable housing is effective in reducing other social problems. Offering case management from one organization, rather than multiple organizations, can help in coordinating approaches to address underlying issues. Additionally, I believe that providing 24 hr mental health care access (even from the local clinics), which contributes to other disease like domestic violence, increases in homelessness, youth substance abuse, and more. If we are going to prioritize Utah values like strong families, we need to make strong investments in helping all community members achieve those standards. Also, the Health Department has several programs in place that attempt to address mental health, in several different places. However, basic psychological-trauma awareness is absent in our community. As a trauma survivor myself, I do forwarding and offer individual therapeutic trauma support for free to those in our community that may be suffering from emotional disturbances or traumatic stress disorders, mood, and social disruption. This is a simple approach that helps train community liaisons to provide various phones, residents, death, and more. Allocating such a very small amount of the budget to trauma awareness should help people understand what is going on and how to heal. This, in turn, would turn to the community's benefit as a whole. Environment: another, I would like to suggest the city invest more into helping community members create environmentally-sustainable environments, starting at a local level. Things as simple as funding for small neighborhood gardens that give more support. We see a lot with a bike, honesty, and there are other options available to parents & students who do not feel like they are getting a quality education. If students and teachers have submitted feedback about what they need for a meaningful education, we should be willing to listen and fund that. Also, as a graduate from the University of Utah (my bachelors and masters degree), I continue to hope that investments will continue to be supported in access from parents, educators, and students alike, and see what responds they can realistically fulfill. This might require changing what we fund in general! But I believe that at least if we target our change to produce a better future for the young people in our community, while also supporting the teachers and educators that are doing this challenging work financially clearly, we'll pay for it later on. Thank you for reviewing my email, and have a beautiful day! Sincerely, Spencer

subject: A city for people, not cars
comment: Council members, I'm writing in support of updating off-street parking regulations. Specifically, I support a decrease in minimum required off-street parking spaces. Too much of our city is dedicated to infrastructure dedicated to cars, which increases housing costs and decreases walkability. The updated off-street parking regulations would encourage housing, biking, and public transit use Besides. If space dedicated to parking cars was reduced it could be used for additional housing or green space, both of which would make Salt Lake City a better place to live and work. While considering the updated off-street parking regulations, I hope you also consider eliminating minimum parking requirements entirely.
